title: Al-Aqsa in Jerusalem
hook: the farthest mosque in Jerusalem, named third in the hadith of the three mosques

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, raised beside his home, where he now rests, near the Rawdah. Your line was his mosque. Did a blessing on him cross your lips? Day one thousand thirty-seven.

On a wide stone platform in the Old City of Jerusalem, two buildings catch the light. One wears a golden dome; we met it months back, the Dome of the Rock, a shrine built over the rock. The other is lower and longer, at the southern end, with a plainer gray dome. The gold tends to steal the eye. But the long building at the far end is where the rows form on a Friday, shoulder to shoulder, facing south toward Mecca. Its name comes straight out of a verse of the Qur'an. Today: Al-Aqsa in Jerusalem.
screen: `ONE PLATFORM, TWO BUILDINGS.` → `THE GOLD DOME IS THE SHRINE.` → `THE ROWS FORM AT THE FAR END.`

segments.voice: Start with the verse. Surah seventeen opens with the Night Journey of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. In Pickthall's translation, God carried His servant by night "from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship." The Inviolable one is the mosque in Mecca. The Far Distant one, in Arabic al-masjid al-aqsa, is the farthest mosque. The verse gave the place its name. Notice what the verse leaves out: it never names Jerusalem. Muslims have understood the Far Distant place as the mosque there. Second, the list we heard two days ago. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says not to set out on a special journey except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque in Mecca, the Prophet's own mosque in Medina, and al-Aqsa. Jerusalem is named third, and this week has walked them in that order. Third, an older link. Another hadith tells of a companion, Abu Dharr, who asked which mosque was set up first on earth. The answer: the Sacred Mosque. And then? Al-Aqsa. The two are paired from the start. Fourth, the name stretches. Some people use al-Aqsa for the long prayer hall alone. Others use it for the whole walled enclosure, courtyards, trees, the Dome of the Rock and all, which is also called the Noble Sanctuary. The same hill is holy to Jews, who call it the Temple Mount, and the city is dear to Christians. A crowded holiness, and a reason people of more than one faith pray for its peace.
screen: `THE FAR DISTANT PLACE OF WORSHIP.` · `THE THIRD OF THREE MOSQUES.` · `PAIRED WITH MECCA FROM THE START.` · `A HALL, OR THE WHOLE SANCTUARY.` · then, large: `THE FARTHEST MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: The practice: hold Jerusalem in mind for two minutes. Settle, and breathe. Let the city come to you as a place, not a headline: stone streets, bells and calls to prayer, families buying bread, children on their way to school, worshippers of more than one faith passing in the same lanes. Breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for peace and safety for Jerusalem and everyone who lives there. If you don't, simply wish them well, one face at a time. The bell holds the time.
Al-Aqsa, the farthest mosque named in the Qur'an's verse of the Night Journey, and third in the hadith of the three mosques. Today's word.
Your line: the farthest mosque. Today, when you hear Jerusalem in the news, stop for one breath and wish the whole city peace before you scroll on. Day one thousand thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims who can travel to Jerusalem often pray at al-Aqsa, and those who cannot remember it in their prayers and in the story of the Night Journey, recited from Surah al-Isra.

the verse of the Night Journey

myth: the golden dome is the al-Aqsa prayer hall
the gold dome is the Dome of the Rock, a shrine. the prayer hall is the long building with the gray dome.
the Night Journey verse names a Far Distant Place of Worship, not the city
it never says Jerusalem. Muslims have understood the Far Distant place as the mosque there.
the name al-Aqsa was invented long after the Qur'an
it comes straight from the Night Journey verse: the far distant place of worship.

fork.setup: you're Abu Dharr. you've asked the Prophet which mosque was set up first on earth, and he's told you: the Sacred Mosque. what do you ask next?
fork.reveal: he asks "and then which?" and the answer is al-Aqsa. in the hadith the two are paired from the start.

original.note: Arabic: the farthest mosque, the name the Night Journey verse gives the place.

trapdoor: what you thought: al-Aqsa is the mosque with the golden dome.
what it means: the farthest mosque, named in the Night Journey verse; the gold dome next to it is the Dome of the Rock.
what a scholar hears: al-aqsa can mean the long prayer hall alone or the whole Noble Sanctuary, and the hadith of the three mosques names it third.

sources.quoted: from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship

notes: Claims rule: the outline's 'third holiest in Islam' is rendered as 'named third' in the hadith of the three mosques (Bukhari 1189), which names the three in that order. The 'forty years' between the two mosques in Bukhari 3366 is left out.
Pickthall 17:1 fragment quoted from memory; confirm exact wording and capitalization.
Hadith numbers 1189 (three mosques) and 3366 (Abu Dharr: first mosque) should be checked against the numbering used for this path.

Al-Aqsa as the prayer hall vs. the whole compound (al-Haram al-Sharif, 'Noble Sanctuary'); and the brief neutral mention that the site is the Temple Mount for Jews. Confirm the framing is fair and non-political.

Editor pass: the three-mosques hadith and the early prayer toward Jerusalem were both taught on day 1035, so the hadith is now a short callback, the qibla sentence and its 2:142–144 source are cut, and the 'ranking' wording is softened to 'list'. Added that the verse itself does not name Jerusalem, and swapped the repeated three-mosques myth item for one on that point.
Hook says the gray dome is 'plainer'; the dome has been lead/silver-gray in recent times. Confirm.

Audit (2026-10-01): hook said the Dome of the Rock was met 'some weeks back', but it was taught on days 903–905, about four months earlier; changed to 'months back'. Quotations and hadith numbers (Bukhari 1189, 3366) checked.
